pages.text: Two days before the circuit inter-schools athletics trials, Kofi stood beside the 200-metre track feeling unusually small. Several JHS 3 boys had shot up over the past year, their shoulders broader and their voices deeper. Kofi’s own growth spurt had barely begun. Behind the sports pavilion, Baffour held out a dark plastic bottle. “Drink half of this before Friday’s heats,” he whispered. “Energy drink, with a painkiller tablet crushed inside. You will not feel tired at all. Everyone chasing a medal uses a booster.” Kofi looked at the bottle. He badly wanted to keep up with the big boys. For a moment, his hand almost moved.

pages.alt: Behind a school sports pavilion, a taller older student offers an unlabelled dark plastic bottle to thirteen-year-old Kofi in a green athletics vest.

pages.text: Then Kofi stepped back and walked over to Esi and Ibrahim under the neem tree. Esi frowned. “That bottle cannot give you energy, Kofi. We learned why in Science. Your muscles get energy from cellular respiration: cells break down glucose from food, and they release the most energy when they use oxygen. Caffeine itself provides no nutritional energy. It stimulates the brain mainly by blocking adenosine, a chemical that helps us feel sleepy. That can increase alertness and reduce the feeling of fatigue, but it may also cause a racing heartbeat, anxiety or sleep problems, especially in excess. And nobody knows what that tablet is. If it is a strong painkiller such as tramadol, it is worse: it dulls the pain signals that warn you. You could tear a muscle, collapse from the heat, or even have a seizure before you feel anything wrong.”

pages.text: Later that morning in Social Studies, Madam Mensah taught a lesson on adolescent development and peer pressure. “During puberty, hormones such as testosterone in boys and oestrogen in girls trigger growth spurts,” she explained. “Each body follows its own normal timetable. Comparing yourself with an older classmate makes you feel insecure for no good reason—and negative peer pressure feeds on that insecurity.” Assertiveness, she said, means holding your ground calmly. On the board she wrote three steps: say a firm “No” without apologising, state the harm plainly, and walk away towards supportive friends or a trusted adult.

pages.alt: Madam Mensah teaching a JHS class beside a chalkboard showing normal adolescent growth curves and three numbered assertive refusal steps.

pages.text: In the last period, RME, the class discussed how moral choices test character when no referee is watching. Ibrahim raised his hand. “In Islam, life and a clear mind are sacred trusts. Anything that intoxicates the mind or harms the body is forbidden, whatever nickname people give it.” Esi agreed. “Christians are taught that our bodies belong to God, so we should practise self-control and win honestly.” Kofi remembered what his grandmother often said in Twi about suban pa—good character. It outlasts every trophy won by cheating.

pages.text: After closing, Baffour blocked Kofi near the school gate. “Are you scared, small boy? Or do you want our school to lose?” Kofi steadied his breathing and used Madam Mensah’s steps. “No, Baffour. I do not know what is in that bottle. Unknown tablets mixed with energy drinks can harm the heart and the nervous system. I am not putting that into my body.” This was assertiveness, not anger. He did not argue or trade insults. He walked straight with Ibrahim to Madam Mensah’s office and quietly reported the bottle, so that nobody would collapse on Friday.

pages.alt: At the school gate, Kofi stands upright with a calm, firm open hand refusing the dark bottle while Ibrahim stands supportively at his side.

pages.text: Madam Mensah and the Physical Education master acted quietly before race day. They confiscated the mixture and arranged health counselling for Baffour, without shaming him in public. On Friday, Kofi ran on boiled yam and kontomire stew from the evening before, clean water, and eight hours of sleep. He took the curve of the 200 metres smoothly and finished a proud second—enough to make the circuit team for the district games. Crossing the white line strong and clear-headed, he knew his real victory had been won two days earlier.

activities.question: Why is it scientifically wrong to call caffeine mixed with an unprescribed painkiller an "energy booster"?
options: Caffeine provides the same energy as glucose and slows the heartbeat
Painkillers convert directly into protein and water inside leg muscles
Muscles need food glucose for energy; caffeine only stimulates alertness

activities.question: Why had several JHS 3 boys developed broader shoulders and deeper voices earlier than Kofi?
options: Pubertal hormones trigger normal growth spurts at different ages in adolescents
Younger students do not carry out cellular respiration until JHS 3
Only athletes who take supplements experience puberty

activities.question: Which action demonstrates assertive refusal when facing negative peer pressure?
options: Shouting insults and starting a fight behind the sports pavilion
Say a firm No, name the risk plainly, walk away, and alert a trusted adult
Accepting the bottle to avoid teasing and hiding it in a schoolbag

activities.question: Apply it: The night before an exam, a classmate offers Ama an unlabelled "brain tablet" to stay awake. What is the best response?
options: Refuse firmly, decline unknown tablets, and stick to her revision plan
Take half a tablet to be polite
Accept it and keep it in her bag for later

activities.prompt: Put Kofi’s responsible decision-making steps in chronological order.
items: Baffour pressures Kofi to drink an unlabelled concoction with painkillers.
Esi explains that cellular respiration, not stimulants, gives real energy.
Kofi recalls refusal skills, self-control, and the value of suban pa.
Kofi calmly refuses the bottle and alerts Madam Mensah confidentially.

activities.definition: Expressing one’s values, rights, and boundaries calmly and firmly without aggression or passive surrender.
distractors: Bullying younger students into following orders
Agreeing silently with unsafe behaviour to fit into a group

glossary.definition: The biochemical process inside cells that breaks down glucose (with oxygen in aerobic respiration) to release usable energy.
A naturally occurring chemical messenger involved in sleepiness; caffeine blocks some of its receptors and can temporarily increase alertness.
The developmental stage during adolescence when hormones trigger rapid growth and reproductive maturity.
Communicating a clear, respectful "No" or personal boundary firmly without hostility or apology.
An Akan concept meaning upright character, self-discipline, and honourable conduct.
